Review from the perspective of a dad with very limited time:

Honestly, a terrible choice if you’re looking for a quick gaming session.
A single run can take up to 40 minutes, and since you cannot pause the game, this becomes a real problem — especially in Duo or Trio.

You cannot simply pause an online multiplayer game!
So be warned: you need a proper time slot to play this game in peace. This is not a “jump in for 10 minutes” kind of experience.

That said:
It takes a while to get used to the pace — but once it clicks… oh boy, this game absolutely slaps.
The power spikes hit hard, and when everything comes together, it feels insanely good.

Despite the time commitment issues:
9/10 Soulslike — amazing gameplay, just not parent-friendly.

Still boggles my mind how a game with this much replayability got a SINGULAR dlc.

While this game does suffer from a lot of missed potential, ELDEN RING NIGHTREIGN and its DLC provide hundreds of hours of fun; it easily kept my friends and I hooked and grinding for months. The main idea of NIGHTREIGN is to condense the classic ELDEN RING experience down into a 45 minute run with randomized bosses, points of interest and weapons, and make it cooperatively playable up to 3 people.

ELDEN RING NIGHTEIGN isn't exactly a roguelike, but it definitely plays like one. And a kind of weak one, at that. It's not a big deal at all when you first start playing, but becomes more apparent as you rack up hours. This game's biggest flaw is its lack of randomization in its experiences, leading to fatigue and runs ultimately not feeling significantly different from each other. This problem is helped by the addition of the  DLC's content, but there are still many "What If?" moments. What if they could have added Shadow of the Erdtree weapons? What if there were twice as many legacy Dark Souls bosses? What if the POI's weren't so formulaic? If you are a massive roguelike fan, you may find other games in the genre to far surpass NIGHTREIGN's random elements. 

Basically everything else is so great though. The FROMSOFT combat and gameplay formula is more fun than ever, with new additions to the sandbox unique to NIGHTREIGN. The super sprint added brings the pace up to a blistering level and it's addicting to dart around the map.  All playable characters are so much fun to play and master, with different costumes to acquire and relics to customize your loadout. All the bosses pose a feasible challenge and remain a blast to learn. 

NIGHTREIGN's best aspect are the ten final NIGHTBOSSES. They are completely original bosses with insane spectacle, challenge, and sense of reward for overcoming. Taking on each one and finally managing to conquer them alongside two friends still hasn't lost its luster. These are some of the greatest bosses FROMSOFT have ever created. Most of them have an alternate 'hard mode' version, with difficulty cranked to 11 and insane alternate movesets. 

Post launch, FROMSOFT added a "ranked mode" called Deep of Night, and it provides a massive challenge as well. This hard mode, alongside the added "hard mode" bosses offer tons of replayability. This game is an absolute blast, and will remain in rotation with my friends for a while. 

If you can't get enough FROMSOFT and you have a few friends willing to take the plunge, this is an easy recommend.

I am leaving this negative review because FromSoftware and Bandai Namco have completely abandoned Elden Ring Nightreign.

This game has a brilliant cooperative and roguelite foundation, but it severely lacks variety. We are feeling completely left behind. We supported this project from day one, and instead of giving it the long-term content and updates it deserves, the developers dropped a couple of minor patches and walked away to focus on other franchises.

Just because FromSoftware has achieved massive success with Dark Souls and the main Elden Ring game doesn't mean they can treat players of their spin-offs as secondary customers. This absolute lack of post-launch support heavily damages the studio's prestige and reputation.

We DO NOT WANT this game to die. We demand substantial content updates, more boss variety, classes, or whatever. Until FromSoftware shows they care about this community and adds real content, this review will remain negative.

Man, this is a tough one. There is a lot to love here for Elden Ring fans, but I'd say the game misses it's mark overall.

Obviously, you've got the same fantastic Elden Ring combat. Plenty of familiar bosses are here, and in particular there are a few from the Dark Souls franchise which I thought was an awesome addition. Characters are extremely diverse and allow you to approach your favorite play-styles in unique ways when incorporating the special characters abilities. There is a character here for most everyone, and its fun to switch it up and improve at all of them. Nightlords are, for the most part, really fun and engaging fights that demand your attention and teamwork (there are some stinkers though, you know the ones). Leveling system being more streamlined compliments the new faster-paced gamplay nicely. And skins are pretty cool overall too. 

BUT.....there is not even close to enough variation in content here. Build variety is technically there but so many effects and passives are just boring and enhance your character in the most minuscule ways. Relics are just like the effects; there are a FEW interesting ones but by and large they are boring and unneeded for success in the game. Honestly, by the time you have beaten all the Nightlords for the first time, you will have seen basically the entire game. The amount of map seeds in the game is a JOKE, and the boss pool is laughably small considering all the bosses they could have used but didn't. The 'rare' occurrences in the game are quite frankly TOO rare, to the point where you almost never see them in any given session. Then, instead of maybe adding more stuff to the game, they made Deep of Night mode instead, which is an absolute grind-a-thon that gets unendingly frustrating even as early as Depth 2.

We're SOOOO close guys! This is a fun and engaging Elden Ring spin-off, but it is BEGGING for more variety. I have had fun with it, enough for me to still leave a positive review, but saying I recommend it would be a huge overstatement. Give it some time to cook if you are on the fence, hopefully the upcoming DLC will fix some of these problems.

[h1]Good Spinoff, Bad Roguelite[/h1]

I always have a mixed feeling towards Elden Ring Nightreign. The extraction-style gameplay shuns me away for quite a while. But after playing it through, I certainly feel less dismissive about it. On one hand, it's admirable to see FromSoft step out of their comfort zone and try something different. Yet on the other hand, Nightreign is not a particularly good roguelite experience. Even some of the indie brethren can eclipse its effort. Still, Nightreign is an interesting experiment on mixing up different mechanics from popular genres. It's better to bring a friend or two along. Solo is certainly doable, but the learning curve is steep.

[h2]Thing I Like About Elden Ring Nightreign:[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]The Raids:[/b] Now I think about it. The Radahn fight in the base game is definitely the prototype behind Nightreign. You and your friends working together to take on (or cheese the hell out of) a big boss is one of the best moments in the Souls series. Nightreign tries to expertize this experience, and I say it's a job well-done. Scout the map, plan the route, conquer locations, loot the gear, run away from the shrinking zone, defeat two ring bosses, tackle the Nightlord and fail miserably (prerequisite). A complex process on the surface, but with friends you can easily make it fun. Moreover, teamwork has never been more important than ever. Who draws aggro, who deals damage, and when to rotate the roles for breathing room, [strike] and stop going after the Bell-bearing A-hole[/strike] are key to a successful expedition.

[*][b]Preset Characters:[/b] I am a little bit sad you can't create your own character, but at least the eight available ones are very unique. Each of them offers a distinctive playstyle and fulfills a certain role in your team. You can find your preferred playstyle in these characters. Moreover, their backstories are also interesting, told through FromSoft's usual storytelling shenanigans, except this time it's rather clear and more involved in the player's part. I like how these people feel like a bunch of misfits bound together by a shared goal. Yet, through remembrance you can easily see how their fate intertwined with each other. 

[*][b]Combat QOL Improvements:[/b] Now these are something that sparks excitement not only for the game but also for future titles. Nightreign has a lot of improvements on both combat and movement. Instant sprint offers a new way to close gaps and make distance. Jump has been even better at dodging attacks since the inclusion of kick/wall jump. Enemies' grab attacks are now unifyingly color-coded for easier recognition. There's also a red marker on the character indicating who is being targeted by the boss right now. Performing a critical attack no longer makes the enemies invulnerable, meaning your teammates can continuously wail on their downfalls. Whips, shields, and even bows can now backstab, and so on.
[/list]

[h2]Things I Like And Dislike About Elden Ring Nightreign:[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]Shifting Earth:[/b] Nightreign's map is pretty stale. The random generation doesn't alter the map layout much, so the developers create this feature to mitigate the problem. Unfortunately, Shifting Earth only achieved half of its goal. For the good parts, these new biomes drastically change parts of Limveld. They offer new terrains, special points of interest and a unique secret buff for you to uncover. However, the way the developers implement leaves a lot to be desired. They are randomized one "period" at a time. The game rolls one event, and the next few runs you will always have this event active (unless you sleep). These new terrains also suffer from the same issue as the mainland—fixed placement and fixed layout. I really wish their locations could be randomized, and the other terrains could have the chance to spawn as sub-areas. 

[*][b]Nightlords:[/b] Just like the eight playable characters, all eight Nightlords are fantastic in their own way. The classic orchestral bombardment is in full force. Their presentations are easily the most stunning out of all the Souls series. Their move sets are designed to deal with multiple targets at once, and there are actual interesting mechanics woven in to make the fights more dynamic. The only thing I really dislike about the boss design is the cinematic attack—you know, the one where you see the boss fly away and you wait for almost 10 seconds until it lands that one attack. This is a trend I wish Fromsoft would refrain from using too much. It only works once. The second and third times onward just feel like a waste of time. Oh, and also fck Maris.
[/list]

[h2]Things I Dislike About Elden Ring Nightreign:[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]Relics:[/b] It's farming blood gems in Chalice Dungeons all over again...except it's worst and takes longer to get. I believe the purpose of the relics is to make your early game as smooth as possible. If that's the case, then there are two problems. First of all, the pool is heavily diluted by tons of weak or borderline useless attributes. Even if you manage to roll a stat-boosting one, the number is still too negligible to make a difference. Second, everything is completely randomized. There is no way to reroll attributes, so the only way to get better relics is gambling. 

[*][b]Builds:[/b] This might be me not adjusting my mindset accordingly, so take it with a grain of salt. Despite introducing character abilities and passive bonuses, the build flexibility is surprisingly rigid in Nightreign. One of the beautiful things in Souls games is how easily and freely you can change your build. Nightreign doesn't do that. All characters have set stats, and leveling up gives a universal increase to every stat. As a result, it's easier to lean into what the character is already capable of instead of exploring other possibilities. Passives on weapons might enable a certain degree of availability, but it will never be half as good as a dedicated build. 
[/list]

[b]中文小簡評[/b]
一開始《艾爾登法環黑夜君臨》讓我五味雜陳，強調快速清塔撿裝躲圈的設計與FromSoft一貫照自己步調細細探索的作風大相逕庭，讓我望之卻步，直到夏特才決定入手來體驗，把玩幾場後我算是體悟出箇中滋味。《黑夜君臨》是FromSoft踏出舒適圈的一次大膽嘗試，將既有的魂系戰鬥與現今較熱門遊戲類別的機制加以融合，的確打造出獨具風味的遊戲體驗，這份勇氣值得嘉許。然而以roguelite的角度去看的話機制非常不成熟，幾乎被其他獨立同儕輾壓。不過最好還是拉個朋友一起入坑，單人打可行，就是學習曲線過於坎坷。

[b]喜歡的點[/b]
[list]
    [*]現在想來，《艾爾登法環》裡的碎星Boss戰應該就是《黑夜君臨》的藍圖吧！和朋友一起挑戰（或用各種外鄉手段）打Boss絕對是魂系遊戲中最最棒的體驗之一。《黑夜君臨》在這點上就發揮的淋漓盡致，一起觀察地形、一起規劃路線、一起分工、一起跑圈撿裝、一起打黑夜王然後再一起被壓在地上磨擦。
    [*]這也是歷代魂系中最講究團隊合作的重要性，誰負責坦傷、誰負責輸出、何時要輪替吸仇恨製造喘息空間、誰要去阻止隊友在等級太低的情況下還敢去打鈴珠獵人和龍形大樹守衛，這些流程看似複雜，但和朋友一同經歷就能充分享受其中樂趣。
    [*]不能自創角色有點可惜，但遊戲提供的八位主角各具特色，各自擁有鮮明的定位與專精的武器，絕對能讓你找到自己心儀的玩法。此外，他們的背景故事也很有趣，除了FromSoftware一往的敘事手法外，也加入了許多互動要素，讓你能更清楚了解他們。我意外地滿喜歡這群看似格格不入的烏合之眾，只是因為共同的目標而聚集在一起。然而，透過追憶你就能明白他們彼此的命運緊密交織在一起。
    [*]不過我最喜歡的還是本作在戰鬥方面做的各種改良，像是瞬間衝刺讓你能快速逃離或拉近與Boss間的距離、、敵人抓技有用更鮮明的特效顯示、Boss打出大招時也能清楚看出誰被鎖定、爆擊或背刺敵人時隊友可以無視無敵禎盡情輸出等，這些都是很棒的設計，讓人非常期待FromSoft未來遊戲的走向。
[/list]

[b]又愛又恨的點[/b]
[list]
    [*]《黑夜君臨》的地圖變化隨機性低且非常單調，通常走過一次就能輕鬆記起來，因此製作團隊想用「特異地形」來做點變化，我只能說這項設計只做到一半。先說優點，特異地形的確有效改變部分主地圖的地形，加入了新敵人、新地點以及專屬隱藏增益讓你能在規劃路線上做些改變。但是呢，特異地形是以隨機「週期性」的方式出現， 一旦條件生成你接下來的所有行動都會是出同一個地形，而且這些特異地形也跟主地圖有同樣的問題：位置與分部始終固定，沒有隨機地點，也沒有隨機生成特殊子區域實屬可惜。
    [*]黑夜王的表現各有千秋，氣勢與演出絕對不輸FromSoft過去的經典Boss，配樂一個比一個還有特色，招式上不僅充分考量「一對多」的要素，也成功融入有趣且非一面倒的機制，這在正統魂系中可是非常少見的。缺點的話，我覺得FromSoft可以少用點浮誇的攻擊，這裡是指那種Boss會突然走遠遠的開始搞一些很炫泡的前置，然後過來打你一下。第一次感覺很新鮮很壯麗，但兩、三次後難免會覺得有點浪費時間。
[/list]

[b]不喜歡的點[/b]
[list]
    [*]遺物機制根本就是下位版的金盃刷血寶石啊！即使退一萬步說遺物的功能只是用來讓你前期好過一些好了，詞條全靠隨機生成，既沒有鎖詞條重刷其他欄位的功能，還將一些改變角色技藝或絕活的重要詞條與一堆非常無用的詞條放在一起，讓人刷起來非常氣餒。
    [*]這點應該歸究於我個人心境還沒調適過來。《黑夜君臨》看似有許多被動與技能可搭配，實際上角色流派的多樣性與變化性比想像中來的侷限。本作不像《艾爾登法環》可以隨時隨地改變配點裝備，角色初始數值固定，升等也自動幫你配好點，與其探索其他可能性倒不如更專心玩角色已經擅長的流派。
[/list]

It’s the experience with your FRIENDS

Everyone shouting to kill the boss, blaming each other for doing smth random shi-, someone pulling extra enemies, someone refusing to revive because they’re busy looting

Now the DLC, Forsaken Hollows
The bosses are honestly incredible
Some of the best FromSoftware has made. Fast, aggressive, and actually fun to learn (like ED balancers and Dreglord)

Easily the highlight of the DLC

Simple locations somehow turn into a full expedition
You spend half the time just figuring out how to reach things instead of actually doing them
At the end of the day, Nightreign is a really solid roguelite co-op game
Not perfect, not balanced all the time, but ridiculously fun if you’ve got friends to suffer through it with
I’d still give it a 8/10.

Nightreign is the premier "I want to play a SOULS game, but I don't want to commit to an entire playthrough" game. It's quick, it's challenging, it has enough content to satisfy people who get bored with things quickly, and it has enough depth to squeeze several hundred hours out of it for the people who really want to dig in. At the time of this review, I have a save file with 160 hours with all achievements that has reached Depth 4, without the Forsaken Hollows DLC.

If the gameplay trailers don't sell the concept well: Nightreign is a fast-paced cooperative Roguelite boss rush where the core gameplay loop is a run that takes anywhere from 15 to 50 minutes (average 40 mins) depending on how fast or slow you win or lose. You select a Nightfarer, a character that comes with their own unique abilities and stat spreads, and then you group with up to two other players to challenge one of the Nightlords of your choice. During the run, you have two 'days' to search the map for ways to get stronger: enemies killed grant you level ups, and bosses killed grant you randomly generated weapons or permanent buffs. After 7 minutes of daytime, your play area will gradually shrink, forcing you to maneuver towards a zone where you fight a more powerful boss. After defeating the boss, the 'day' ends, your play area resets, and the next 'day' begins. On the third day, you do not get any more chances to grow stronger, and instead are thrown into a fight against the final boss of the run: a Nightlord. Regardless of win or loss, you are awarded with a currency and a few relics (permanent upgrades that persist through runs), though victory always rewards more.

In the base game, there are 8 Nightlords, 5 maps, and 8 Nightfarers (6 at the start, two unlocked later). The Nightlords are tricky enough that they take multiple attempts to master, the maps have enough hidden secrets that you'll still find something new every run, and the Nightfarer's abilities provide a lot of room for mastery, such that even after 100 hours you'll still be learning new techniques. Seven of the Nightlords come with more difficult variants, known as "Everdarks", that pose a significantly greater challenge over their base form.

The worst part of the game is easily the lobby area and the meta progression. The Roundtable Hold is a place where you spend resources earned in a run towards unlocking permanent power-ups for your future runs, or where you unlock cosmetic items for your Nightfarers. Each Nightfarer comes with their own mini-story, told in the form of "Remembrance" quests that have 4-5 steps each, and they're just long enough to give some charm to what would otherwise just be caricatures of popular Souls builds. However, there isn't as much depth-of-lore present in Nightreign as compared to other Fromsoft titles. After about 100 hours, the lobby becomes a place where you either spend all your currency on relic gacha where you have a miniscule chance to generate a random relic that synergizes well with itself, or a place where you parkour idly after having exhausted all of the NPC's dialogue as you wait for a match to be found.

The late game experience revolves around a hard mode called Deep of Night, which features scaling difficulty and skill based matchmaking. Enemies deal more damage (and stronger variants appear), items found in a run have stronger text but also come with downsides, and unlike the regular mode, your map and your Nightlord (or Everdark Nightlord) are randomly chosen. Victory in Deep of Night will increase your rating until you eventually reach a greater Depth where the challenges scale up even more. Deep of Night runs grant you more currency and will generate more powerful relics that can only be used for Deep of Night runs. I have more than 1000 hours across the entire Souls series, and have beaten many of the games deathless or at soul level 1, but clearing Depth 3 has been personally more challenging than anything else i've done before.

TL;DR this is a really great game to casually play with friends that does not require a huge time commitment, but also provides a seriously challenging experience to anyone who wants to lock in. HOP ON NIGHTREIGN

review:
Elden Ring, but a lot faster.

If you like the combat from the souls / Elden Ring games, you’ll love this.

If you like the slow exploration / discovery of those games, you might not like this.

There are 8 characters (plus 2 from the DLC) that you can pick. Each has their own special abilities + passive bonuses.

Each ‘run’ has 2 nights where you go from POI to POI collecting loot, clearing out enemies, and collecting extra power from bosses. On the 3rd and last night, you’ll face a nightlord (super boss). After you win / lose a run, you’ll collect relics that can add passive bonuses to your characters. So far I have yet to see anything overpowered like other roguelikes, but I usually only play solo and I’m bad. 

For the solo players, yes it is doable - the enemies scale to the amount of players and in solo the enemies take turns on aggro so usually you won’t get ganked. 

Do I recommend it for solo play?

Yes - only if you have patience. You will fail a lot unless you are good at these games. I have only one win in my 15 or so hours played. I am still really enjoying the updated movement and combat.

Highly recommend that you make some friends and play together in voice chat - makes the game way more enjoyable imo.

EDIT: Random trios can actually be fun sometimes. I was skeptical at first because I've never played multiplayer in these types of games, but it's actually enjoyable when you have tm8s that have more than 2hrs played. Highly recommend playing solo a bit and learning the game, then playing online. ymmv

I really wasn't sold on the idea of Nightreign at first, but after getting into the game with a friend it's quite addicting. Nightreign condenses the fun parts of Elden Ring into a cheaper, bite sized adventure; I only wish they dedicated harder to the rougelite experience.

I was really into Elden Ring when it first came out, I did about nine playthroughs back to back and did one hundred percent completion, though I've tried revising the game since and just can't get into it the same way. Open worlds never really were for me and upon returning to the game it's really pushed me away, I want to get to the fun stuff and not spend more time horsing around getting from place to place, collecting everything I need for my character. Nightreign is the solution to this; it sections off the map and shows you clearly where things are, minimizing the downtime and maximizing the fun stuff.

Unlike Elden Ring, Nightreign isn't an RPG, instead of a custom character and build you have preset characters with specialities and unique skills, which like a lot of things in this game don't sound like they'd work but in practice really do. Each character feels unique and like they have a role on the team, my only issue in this department is the lack of representation of some build types. There isn't really a dedicated miracle character, you've got Revenant sort of but unlike Recluse there's no way for her to get mana back and while she is still my favourite character, she doesn't really feel like a second caster. More characters are promised as DLC but we're yet to see any so far.

One big shortcoming of Nightreign is the lack of wack. Rougelites and roguelikes alike are typically full of upgrades that really let you push the game to its breaking points which is part of the fun; but here they're very shy and reserved about letting things get too crazy. The vast majority of upgrades you'll collect are very minor things like "stamina recovery +4" or "physical attack +6%," the craziest upgrades you'll find see is something like raining fire or magic stars when you're walking which is as useless as it sounds unfortunately. I would love to see stuff like faster attack speed or lower attack interval buffs, or even more out there things like leaving a trail of fire behind you when you run or something.

Elden Ring Nightreign is a somewhat experimental game with a lot of ideas that sometimes feels like they were holding back. If you like soulslike games but don't always want to do a full new playthrough because the tedious parts weigh you down after doing it all multiple times already, Nightreign is the cure. It's got all the meat; plenty of huge, fun boss fights, unique abilities and weapons, and is still receiving free content updates. Unfortunately, no swimsuit outfit for Recluse and Revenant; oh, and we got Alva for Birdman but no Zullie skin for Recluse? Maybe one day....

My review for this game will remain negative until they stop penalizing me in Deep of Night when both other players leave the game. I should not have to play every single match solo just to advance in Deep of Night. It is absolutely ridiculous to lose 200 or more points for leaving a match that both other players already left.

I want to preface that while I don't recommend the game, I do think it is a "good" game. As a player with 1200+ hours on Elden Ring, thousands more consuming content, hundreds of hours on Nightreign, and 12+ years of FromSoft gaming, it's actually really fun to play. However, I can't recommend it for one reason alone, and that can be minimised to one word: undercooked. So while it comes up as red, it's not a BAD review.

(This is not a spoiler-free review, in case you want to be surprised by the game)

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
You have two "days" to run around the map as fast as possible, killing any enemies in your path in order to gain weaponry and passives in hopes of eventually killing the Nightlord, who is the 'final boss' of the run. Each day is segregated by a major boss fight of its own, usually being bosses from Elden Ring and occasionally Dark Souls.
Unlike other entries in the series, you can't make your own character and build here. You're playing as preset characters, all with their own stats, preferred weapons, abilities, and ultimates. You can't crouch and there is no Torrent/horse anymore, but you can sprint really fast and climb walls now. It's actually extremely fun to blitz the map like prime Wally West by yourself.
Getting passives is very much a big part of the rougelike element of the game. Killing bosses, important enemies, and opening some chests will give you a drop that usually has something like two weapons (with minor passives) or a larger passive. Your survival really hinges on you choosing the right things, as these boosts can be extremely significant (like 18% more defense against holy damage, and this is stackable with itself and talismans). At the end of a run, you'll get 'relics' that are equippable passives for every run, like a loadout of sorts. It's pretty close to gacha and is definitely designed to keep you coming back for the perfect relic set.
It's also multiplayer, up to 3 players (which is literally odd). Your success also hinges on their performance to a degree (you can solo carry if you never get hit, but everything has higher health scaling). As an extremely good player in these games, your average player is not going to be the greatest of help (which is fine) and will likely need a lot of ressurections. You can run duo/solo, but the game is definitely best with three.
This is the very basic gameplay loop and doesn't cover everything, but that's the gist.

[h3] The Map [/h3]
It places you in a map that isn't necessarily procedurally generated, as the main map is actually a large set of pre-made seeds. This means with enough playing you can start to recognise exactly what will happen, exactly what boss is behind that gaol, what 'random' events will occur, and exactly what the shopkeep will have.
The game attempts to alleviate this by having a 'Shifting Earth' mechanic that heavily modifies a corner of the map. Day 2 will take place within it, so in a way it's a mini map to explore. The DLC is also a Shifting Earth, except it replaces the entire map instead of a corner and has its own music, enemies, etc. The problem with this is that Shifting Earths are [i] usually [/i] random to get on a run (the DLC one can only be accessed if everyone has the DLC unfortunately), so 70% of the time you are still running around on the same map.

[h3] Other [/h3]
It's hard to split this game up into different categories since so much of this game is both borrowed from other games and nebulous on its own, so I'll just throw in a few things I can think of. Firstly, the music is among some of the best in the entire series. It's like Bloodborne level for sure, surpassing even Elden Ring imo. Caligo, Augur, Balancers, DLC tracks, etc. Those tracks had me floating inside my room. The story seems pretty cool, but I haven't invested myself super deeply into it. The characters are sick and they're almost fully voice acted. Cosmetics are cool, love the Dark Souls skins. The actual character designs are some of my favorite in the series, you'll wish you looked as good and moved as quickly as you do in Nightreign when you go back to Elden Ring.

[h1] The Elephant in the Room [/h1]
Nightreign wants to be a rougelike. This means it is competing with other ones. But I cannot recommend it as a rougelike because the content is so thin. Within 50 hours you will probably have beaten every Nightlord, seen most weapons, and have a gameplay loop. Nothing in the game will surprise you. Build variety is far less complicated here than in Hades, Risk of Rain, Gungeon, Binding of Isaac, anything. You'll run around on the same map, do the same things, and fight the same boss. Why did the DLC not add any weapons from ER/Dark Souls? The game isn't truly random. Base map is 20 seeds, Shifting Earths are 5 more each, and the DLC is probably another 20. The game gets so samey as a rougelike in a way that is so much faster than other ones.

I also can't recommend this to new players as the game is more brutal than past entries. Everything is timed, stats seriously matter, bosses are brutal. I can't recommend this game before any of the original games (Elden Ring, Dark Souls, etc.) because it is more of a hodgepodge rather than a complete experience. This game sits in the awkward niche of players that loved the other games and just want more, even if it's pretty anemic.

This game is an endless well of potential and it's fun as hell, but does absolutely nothing better than other games for me to tell you to buy it. My opinion could change if they update the game again, but who knows. This game is truly delicious stale bread, but it is stale bread nonetheless. Buy it on sale or if you REALLY feel like you are missing out.

Fellow maidenless, 

Nightreign f**king rules. The game is experimental, flawed, but good. I personally don't think it should win GOTY or even get any MP awards at the VGAs this year (and I say this as a massive Fromsoft fan), but I definitely think the game is worth playing if you enjoy Souls games and rogue likes. It’s like Elden Ring Seamless Coop but you don’t have to actually go through the entire open world for an hour between each boss. Every character is well-designed and fun to play. The returning bosses are great and the new Nightlord bosses are some of the best in the series. THEY REMOVED FALL DAMAGE. I see a lot of negativity towards the game. Some of it is fair criticism. But the idea that this is just an asset flip cash grab or the beginning of the end of fromsoft is absurd. If you liked Elden Ring, it’s more Elden Ring, except without all the annoying busywork of Elden Ring, and you can play with your friends or wife’s boyfriend without a mod or the awful souls game co op mechanics.

It's so good. Maybe the hardest game they've put out yet, at least on first pass when solo. It's brutal, but the satisfaction of overcoming a mere single run is enormous. At first, it can feel overwhelming for a solo player, nigh on impossible. Once you've figured out how to manage and coordinate your runs is when the game starts firing on all cylinders. And it's not even a full priced game. You can pick it up for 40$, which at this point, is becoming half the price of a new over budget AAA game.

Nightreign shocked me by having lore and story as well. It has personal quests for each character, that include cutscenes and NPCs around the world's hub in addition to tasks to perform within matches. There are also quite a few endings connected to the remembrances, which are quite fun and interesting to complete. Additionally, there are static set pieces in the game that are added to maps as you progress the game forward, and those include interesting handcrafted level design. They are not as robust as a legacy dungeon, but they are very cool nonetheless. They scratch the itch and include some wild descents and boss fights, all pasted on top of the procedural maps. And lastly, all the original bosses I've encountered so far are fantastic. And each character has brand new move sets (in the form of tactical and ultimate abilities) that are unique to Soulsborne games in general. Oh, and many of the old bosses that are directly reused have new move sets as well. So, even their recycles have had a little bit of dev work.

Honestly, the amount of new development for this game (that isn't even a full-priced game) has impressed me. To each their own, but Nighteign does not remotely resemble shovel ware. It is good and there is fun to be had for sure. But it’s also… a one note game. It does one specific thing and outside of that it is pretty sparse. Which is fine, especially for a budget title, but I have to say I’m pretty underwhelmed with it after beating the final boss in 40 hours. There’s really not much more to the game unless you just love dropping in and doing it all over again. I don’t feel the urge to grind skins or rng for better relics so there’s no real reason to keep playing. Some people will love just playing it over and over which is great but it’s definitely the quickest I’ve put down a fromsoft game. Still, overall it’s a great condensed version of Elden Ring that has you doing all the fun stuff that Elden Ring provides in a frenzy of fighting, looting, and building your character. It’s just a refreshing game in a sea of corporate slop.

Neutral -

Looking back, I didn't care about 'Elden Ring Fortnite' before it launched and yet it is currently my most played game on Steam for good reason (which is why I felt like I should write a review.)

The main selling point is the same as most games by FromSoftware: the sweet taste of victory after struggling against all odds versus brutal bosses through practice and mastery of game mechanics. It never gets old, and Nightreign further makes this even more addicting because you will strive for this with other players; especially ones who are willing to be cooperative and play together as a team.

The whole movement and combat aspects are great, fluid, and you'll almost never have any moment to relax. Learning how to route properly and where certain chests/loot are placed takes a while but it never makes or breaks a run because in the end, your skills matter the most. 

You have 10? Different characters to choose from (DLC included), each with different playstyles which get even more customizable with the relic system. At this point I have played all of them and while some feels better to play than others, every character is viable even at the highest difficulty (Depth 5).

Speaking of which, game difficulty is a tricky metric to measure. I will assure you though, that the base 'story-mode' game could be challenging yet very doable, even for casuals. Dying over and over is expected in these games and you will die a lot while learning how to play better, but when you see how much better you can dodge and punish boss attacks, you'd feel like the greatest player there ever was.

A run typically goes for ~40 minutes so you can just jump in and get off the game without much time investment. Even less if the team wipes during certain mini boss fights within the run, or even longer if your team struggles at the final boss. What I can say is that in those ~40 minutes, you will focus so hard you won't even realize 40 minutes have gone by.

I don't really have anything bad to say about this game, just make sure to have friends or a group to play it with. Random queue can match you with extremely laggy people; not to mention there are quite a few cheaters running about.

All in all, the game is addicting because it's seriously 'dopamine rush' the game. I have 900 hours in the game, I still (mostly) play the same 3 characters over and over again, and I still die a lot :))

[h1]Preface[/h1]
Elden Ring veterans have almost nothing to complain about when it comes to Nightreign. In essence, this title provides more Elden Ring content with added variety, faster pacing, and easy-to-pick-up yet hard-to-master builds and playstyles that provides enough replayability with overall game design that makes it easy to get into another session whenever you have what I call the "Souls itch."

[h1]Positives[/h1]
[b]No Time to Waste[/b]
Before delving into Nightreign, there were two primary concerns I had from what I knew about the game so far: time-limited runs and boss variety. The time-limited runs is a godsend for players like myself who want more Elden Ring but also seek a fresh experience. The exploration is there (albeit with less freedom from the vanilla title), but the balance between the need to explore and focus on boss fights is all in all well executed. Builds can shift drastically after one or two Nightlord kills and each run can feel unique simply based on how the player approaches each run. As with all games, it all comes down to mindset.

[b]Ten Nightfarers, Ten Playstyles[/b]
By this point, most players will settle for the good ol' DR build with most Nightfarer they choose to run. I myself ran mostly solo (a primary reason I held off on Nightreign for so long since solo play was an afterthought a few months into the game's lifespan), and yet with choices like Wylder, Ironeye, and Raider, my runs were not as grueling as I thought they would be. Melee all-rounder, ranged archer, and heavy-hitting bruiser were all on the menu. Now upon completion, I look forward to trying the other Nightfarers to try more technique-based playstyles like the caster-based Recluse and parry-focused Executor. At the end of the day, Nightreign has something for everyone as long as you focus on building each Nightfarer the right - or maybe even wrong - way.

[b]Performance[/b]
I rarely mention this as a forte for game reviews, but with all the performance issues AAA games have been launching with lately, a honorable mention is at very least in order. Nightreign ran flawlessly for me, and that may be due to patches that have been released since launch but the point still stands: FromSoftware rarely, if ever, misses in the optimization department. Combat is quick and responsive even more so than it was in vanilla. And in a title with co op multiplayer being one of its appeals, that's saying something.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
[b]Day Phases[/b]
This is highly subjective, but granting roughly 13-15 real-time minutes for the exploration cycle before the circle starts closing in might be a turnoff for many players. Time is your greatest enemy in Nightreign, and if anything this can simultaneously be considered a positive as it pushes you to think quickly on your feet and work on your decision-making skills/speed. Granted, you have unlimited time for night/boss phases, but a little more leeway might not have hurt for the less initiated. Just a minor gripe on my end, but not a gamebreaker.

[b]Feels...incomplete?[/b]
Perhaps with more dedicated resources, a bigger pull towards ER newcomers, and I daresay more content & horizontal progression(?), I feel the game could have been bigger than it is. As successful as it may have been, many agree that Nightreign just kind of came and went; perhaps not off the grid, but now it's just there for people to enjoy when they feel like coming back to it. Arguably, Nightreign could have started a movement to take the Soulslike genre to the next level entirely, departing from the singleplayer experience we've had for the last decade and causing a chain reaction of games that could give birth to an entirely new genre. But alas, here we are. Nightreign, quite simply put: [i]More Elden Ring[/i].

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Final Verdict: 9/10 A-[/b]
Though not as deep and immersive as the original Elden Ring, Nightreign delivered on its promises and provided the on-the-go Elden Ring experience for veterans and newcomers alike. It may not have been perfect at launch, but FromSoftware has a healthy habit of always striving to satisfy their fans. Patch after patch, they improved solo play and fine-tuned everything they had in place for a memorable experience. Compared to many other companies that recently lose the faith of their supporters with every title they release in this post-2020 era of ongoing hit-and-miss titles, FromSoft remains faithful to its identity and to this day remains in excellent standing with the loyal fanbase. Now, once again, we look forward to what they have in store for us next.

I am not the biggest fan of Elden Ring, Roguelites, or Battle Royale-esque games. . . So what gives? 

Nightreign falls into a strange realm of games I enjoy in the same way I enjoy Monster Hunter, Outer Wilds, and Peaks of Yore. The game thrives on being driven by a player's knowledge of it's semi-static map, enemy placements, PoI layouts, Boss patterns and weaknesses, and semi-obfuscated meta knowledge. When I first started playing I absolutely did not know how to manage the first day of the game, after another run I got to the second day, and after that I made it to the final day with a bit of flailing. 

After about 30 hours I can safely lead most expeditions in the base map to hit enough points on the map to make it close to max level, if not max, with a decent set of gear. The reality of this learning process is not done through in-game tutorialization or looking up guides, but by a natural learning process from letting other people lead me through the game. By making mental notes about how to better optimize my own time, and apply it to games that I'm in. 

That is the crux of this game's joy for me; it's silent community. Able to instill parts of their knowledge on me in order to collectively teach me to be a better player by paying attention to what they're doing that works, and the things that don't. Every run that I go on seems to teach me something new about the map that I didn't know of before, and that always feels like an absolute blast to me. Watching all of this come together to execute a plan driven by the collective knowledge of other players to get through the game's nights. 

Beyond that the exploration, combat mechanics, and bosses are all better designed and feel as though they have a bit more intent behind them than most souls games. The minimalistic building elements mean that you can get in and out of games relatively quick and will pick up on what works and doesn't work in a rather natural way. 

Being that this isn't a PvP game in the slightest the ability to cooperate with others is always fun for me, and I haven't had too much truly awful experiences to say that I've had a bad time outside of the occasional bit of frustration over failing a couple of clutch moments. 

Nightreign is a game that I think will hold a special place in my heart for proving me wrong about a great deal of apprehensions I had going into it, but I think it's worth people's time if they enjoy learning and optimization in games to try to attain a perfect run and mitigating the curveballs it throws you with it's shifting elements.

Elden Ring isn't just my favourite Souls game—it's my favourite game of all time. The biggest reason for that is the incredible amount of variety it offers. Whether it's the hundreds of unique weapons, countless spells/incantations, diverse enemy types, or unforgettable bosses, there is always something new to discover. That's exactly why Nightreign caught my attention. Instead of committing to a single build for the entire playthrough, this game gave me the chance to adapt and experiment with different weapons, while trying different characters, each with their own unique playstyle, abilities, and skills. It provides great replayability, and I genuinely enjoy my time playing this game.

[h2] Positives/PROS [/h2]

[h3] Gameplay- [/h3]
Nightreign is much more fast-paced compared to Elden Ring. You have Surge Sprint, which lets you run faster (just like Torrent, but without him). You can actually climb walls and obstacles in your path, and there is the Spectral Hawk, which helps you traverse long distances quickly. I wish they had added these features to the main Elden Ring too :(.

Every run feels different due to randomized loot. You also get different characters—each Nightfarer has a different playstyle. For example, Ironeye is an archer, while Recluse specializes in sorceries and magic. Every Nightfarer has its own passive ability, Character Skill, and Ultimate Art. After each run, you receive rewards, including Relics (items that contain passive bonuses, effects, and other benefits), which you can equip on your character to gain advantages, and Murk (the in-game currency), which can be used to purchase cosmetics, emotes, Relics, and other items. All of this makes the gameplay enjoyable and provides excellent replayability.

[h3] Bosses- [/h3]
As this game reuses assets from Elden Ring, you will face many of the same enemies and bosses that you already fought in that game. The game also features six returning Dark Souls bosses that are not part of Elden Ring. You will encounter these either at the end of Day 1 or Day 2. But keep all of that aside—if you reach Day 3, you will face the Nightlords, which are completely unique bosses. There are eight of them in total (excluding the DLC), and they are much harder than the regular bosses you have faced in Souls games. They have diverse movesets and can wipe out your entire expedition with their devastating AOE attacks. And oh my God, the music for these Nightlords is just beyond this world. No other Souls game has boss OSTs of this quality. Special mention goes to Caligo, Fulghor, and Libra. I honestly don't know why this game wasn't nominated for Best Soundtrack at TGA 2025. Everything you do beforehand throughout your journey—your builds, upgrades, and teamwork—ultimately leads to this one final challenge, making it incredibly memorable.

[h3] Quality of Life- [/h3]
This game still has approximately 20–35k active players every day. In my experience, Matchmaking usually took only a few seconds, with the longest wait being around 2–3 minutes. This game provides a smooth multiplayer experience with almost no connectivity or network lag issues. At least it's much better than previous FromSoftware games, where the co-op system felt like hell without mods. This was FromSoftware's first proper multiplayer/co-op game, and I think they did a pretty good job. The optimization is just okayish. During chaotic boss fights, or when a Nightlord gets mad and uses its "signature move," FPS fluctuations are very common. And just like Elden Ring, this game is locked at 60 FPS, which is pretty disappointing.

[h2] Negatives/CONS [/h2]
Now this game starts to show its actual disappointments if you put its positives aside for a moment.
-> This game is very fast-paced - You have to make decisions quickly because you don't get enough time for exploration. Each day lasts for about 15 minutes, and during that time you are under constant pressure to gather gear and loot as fast as possible while the safe zone continuously shrinks. You can miss a lot of things if you don't act quickly. This also means that even if you enjoyed Elden Ring, it's not guaranteed that you'll enjoy this game too. If you're the kind of person who likes to explore the world slowly at your own pace, then this game is not for you.
-> The gameplay loop gets repetitive after some time- After you achieve 100% completion, which can take around 40–50 hours at most, there's nothing much left to do other than grinding in Deep of Night mode.
-> You only get one map - Although there are variations with Shifting Earth events and changing boss locations, they don't make enough of a difference. After several hours of playing, you'll know the entire map, and it becomes very predictable and repetitive.
-> No communication tools when playing with randoms - At least they should have added a text chat or voice chat because communication is very important in a PvE co-op game. Right now, the only way to communicate is by marking locations and equipment on the map.
-> This game is not made for solo play - I know the game scales the health of enemies and bosses depending on the number of players, but solo play is still very difficult because you don't get revived. Although you can obtain Wending Grace, which gives you one extra life, the game can still throw two or even three bosses at you at the end of a day.
-> Lack of content - As FromSoftware has now abandoned this game, there have been no updates regarding its future. The community has been asking for a new map, another Nightlord, or even SOTE weapons from Elden Ring (which I also want). But sadly, with the base game and the Forsaken Hollows DLC, Nightreign's journey seems to be over. There's still hope within the community for at least one more update... but for now, it's just "hope." :(

[h2] Should you buy Nightreign if you want to play solo or with randoms? [/h2]
As I mentioned earlier, the game is not well-balanced for a solo playthrough. You have to act fast from the very first day so that you don't end up under-leveled or without good weapons and upgrades. It is very difficult, but some people still manage to do it. If you equip Relics with useful benefits and just "GIT GUD," you can even defeat the Nightlords solo, so yeah, it's ultimately up to you. Playing with randoms is also fun. Sometimes they'll carry you, and sometimes they'll rage quit mid-game lol. The lack of communication tools is the biggest problem when playing with randoms. Still, most players are cooperative and show good teamwork. But if this game had a chat or voice chat option, it would have been much better.

[h2] Final Verdict- [/h2]
This game was just an experimental project by FromSoftware. I know it's not perfect and has many flaws, but this was never meant to be a live-service game. FromSoftware delivering multiple updates and a DLC is more than enough for what this game was intended to be. The community has its own demands, but I think it's time to move on from this game and let them focus on their future titles. I played this game for over 40 hours, but even in that short time, I made a lot of memories with the friend I played duo with. I still remember the day when we finally reached our first Nightlord together after so many attempts. Although we failed, that fight was absolutely dramatic, and I loved every second of that experience. I will still do at least one run every day because I genuinely love this game. I'm even thinking about starting another playthrough of Elden Ring because this game motivates me to do so. I love everything about the world of Elden Ring—the bosses, characters, music, worldbuilding, lore, and the incredible diversity of its weapons, skills, enemies, spells, and so much more. That's exactly why I loved Nightreign, even with all of its flaws.

[h3] "In the end, it was never about surviving the night—it was about wanting to face it again." [/h3]

I [i]really want to[/i] love Nightreign. I’m a huge Souls fan with countless runs across the series, and I own hundreds of roguelikes, so on paper this should be perfect for me. But something just doesn’t click.

The game throws you in fast and expects you to keep up. If you stop for even a moment to read new abilities or compare weapons, you’re either falling behind your teammates or losing levels because you didn’t rush to the next objective. The tutorial barely explains how the game actually works, so it’s easy to wander into bosses way above your level and lose both time and souls trying to recover.

Meta progression is extremely limited for a roguelike. Each character has 3 rune slots, and those runes can roll up to 3 affixes, so your long-term progression is basically just 9 stat quirks. Some of them are cool, but it doesn’t change how limited it all feels. And because item drops are random, you can easily end up stuck with weapon types you don’t want, making some runs feel flat-out worse through no fault of your own.

Communication is another huge miss. Outside of simple map pings, there’s no text chat, no voice chat, nothing. If you’re solo-queuing, coordinating with random teammates is almost impossible.

There are great boss fights here, and moments that remind you why FromSoftware’s combat systems are so beloved. But getting to those moments means pushing through confusing itemization, a lack of build variety, shallow progression, and no real way to communicate.

I want Nightreign to be amazing, but right now it’s unfortunately more frustrating than fun.

A very cool experiment in game design, From treads new ground in the most efficient way possible, reusing large numbers of Elden Ring assets and reconfiguring them into a completely new experience. A little bit like a roguelike, a little bit like a battle royale, Nightreign has you racing against the clock trying to become as powerful as possible across two days before the showdown with the Nightlord on the third day. Defeating the challenge requires you to figure out a route through the semi-randomized map on the fly, avoiding powerful enemies until you've leveled up, hunting down ruins holding weapons with the boss's weakness, deciding whether you're better off going to a mine to upgrade your weapon or going to a high level fight to hope a better weapon drops. Each playable character is similar to a build you might create for an Elden Ring playthrough, but with a set of unique skills and passives that suit that role -- The dedicated caster has an ability that lets her recover spellpower and concoct new spells based on elemental residue, the greatsword warrior has a grappling hook that lets him quickly move in and out of combat range, the hulking tank has an ability that lets him briefly ignore damage and create a massive counterattack. Each character feels very distinctive, much more so than an Elden Ring playthrough, and having to improvise with what you find gives an opportunity to experiment with weapons and spells you'd never touch on such a playthrough. It's not for everyone, the relentless pace can be difficult to get used to, but I think this experiment is a resounding success.

How big is the gap between Depth 4 and Depth 5?

In my personal experience, the main difficulty of Depth 4 lies in the Night King battle. As early as Depth 3, players have figured out how to farm by fighting Sinners. Unless you mess up extremely badly in the early game, you can almost always get through the opening phase. However, starting from Depth 4, squishy classes can no longer tank certain moves from the Night King—sometimes you still die even with full damage reduction stacked.

By the time you reach Depth 5, most players have fought the Night King enough times. Apart from the Ice Dragon and the Fairy boss, it’s really hard to wipe on the other fights. The only thing I fear about the Ice Dragon is the unmarked ground spikes—the ones that only pop up right under your feet the very second they’re about to hit. The other nightmare scenario is just bad RNG: no good damage-related relics, and your teammates are playing classes like Snail or Hermit that can’t interrupt the big cast. Once the Ice Dragon gets its second ultimate off, it’s basically a slow, guaranteed wipe.

Some people say Depth 5 feels no different from Depth 4. If you’re playing squishy classes like Hermit or Snail, you still die from one single hit either way. The only real difference is that Depth 5 drops way better relics. After all, a truly skilled player can clear Depth 5 even without any relics at all—it just takes a lot longer because of the lack of damage.

I'm going to leave this review for those who are like me who love Elden Ring, but might still be on the fence about Nightreign. This is nothing at all like Shadow of the Erdtree or Vanilla. It's more of a spinoff than a real souls game.

Nightreign is a wonderful game for people who enjoy boss rushes/gauntlets, speedrunning, or practicing and refining a plan many times over to perfection. It is fine-tuned to be a dream game for people just like this. It can also be a good activity for people to play a quick pickup game with some friends, since one expedition takes roughly only half an hour, depending on how strong the team is.
Nightreign is a hard pass for people who like exploration, world design, "play at your own pace", slow boss fights using inefficient meme builds, or dungeon style beat-em-up combat over bosses. You will be punished for doing any of this.

Nightreign expects players to be on edge the moment they begin an expedition. You don't have time to read prompts, look at descriptions, test out weapons, or explore non-meta paths if you aren't already moving to another boss area. The fortnite circle closes incredibly fast and you need to be leveling and gearing up as fast as possible to stay ahead. If you fall behind, there is no catchup. You will be behind the rest of the expedition.
Sites of grace automatically levels your character stats. You use sites of grace as checkpoints to run through, rather than as bonfires for resting.

The gameplay loop is like this:
Drop in, Run to the nearest basic enemy (rats or hollows), kill them, run to the nearest site of grace, spam the action key to level up, run to the nearest encampment or easy field boss, level up at a site of grace, repeat until day 3. 
Note that every other basic enemy should be outright ignored for the rest of the game. Fighting them is inefficient and spending too much time on them will cause you to fall behind. I'm honestly not sure why they're even included in the game. We all run past them 100% of the time because we [i] have to. [/i]

If you're thinking that must be some tryhard speedrunning optimization, its not. It's nearly mandatory to do it this way for every expedition. This game is all about boss fights. Clearing field bosses as fast as you possibly can so that you have better odds of beating the night lord boss. This is Nightreign in a nutshell.

With all that being said, I will at least give them credit that I really enjoyed the inclusion of bosses from past souls games. There are tons of easter eggs and references to DS1 and even DS2. It's just such a shame that I really can't tell you much else about the game, because the game encourages you to run past everything and go to the next boss. I don't even remember the designs of a lot of areas in the map (like random events and shifting earth maps). But I can tell you where to pick up another flask at a church ruin, i guess.

The negatives outweigh the positives for me.

It runs and plays like Elden Ring (literally) but in a form of a rogue-like spin-off. It is focused on faster gameplay and online co-op. Nightreign takes 95% of its of weapons, spells and enemy types from base Elden Ring so playing that game first allows you to adapt much faster as you'll know ahead how things work. 

You start each run (expedition) by picking one of 8 (10 with DLC) pre-made characters, there's solo, duo and 3 player party matchmaking options. Each of them takes you on a ~40 min expeditions where you have to survive 2 days and defeat a night lord at the end. Each expedition has semi-randomized gear drops, points of interest and dynamic events. Combat system is the same like in Elden Ring with addition of new faster sprint (that removes the need for mount) and ability to climb walls. Between the expeditions you collect murk (currency) that you can spend on obtaining new relics (passive bonuses) or outfits for the characters.

The plot is as basic as it can be and serves mostly as a background for the gameplay loop. If you just want to play as one character and see the ending credits, the game should take you around 10-15 hours if you succeed most of your expeditions on first attempt. After you complete the story you'll unlock expeditions against stronger versions of most of the bosses as well as "endless night" mode where expeditions get progressively more difficult with each their but you also unlock new slots for build customisation and can find gear with new types of passives and modifiers.

If you enjoy the core gameplay-loop, you can easily get hundreds of hours of content out of this game. I highly recommend it (but also I'm biased towards FROMSOFTWARE games) for people who like action-combat rogue-likes and those who want more of Elden Ring after completing it.

ELDEN RING NIGHTREIGN is an MMORPG roguelike designed for players who love leveling characters and adapting their strategies to dramatic environmental changes in every single run. The combat is intense, driven by various types of monsters, tight time limits and equipment variety

Unlike traditional Souls games, you can’t rely on a specific loadout all the time because the RNG always forces you to change equipment which affects your playstyle. However, you can use gem slots obtained the shop or after finishing run to add new traits that benefit your build and make your runs much more consistent.

While most of the monster return from previous Souls games, they have been adapted perfectly to the game’s mechanics. The community generally knows how to execute a solid run, so there is no need to worry about teammates. If you are new, they will pin the map, lead the way and share loot. Co-op is spectacular, especially with friends, but playing solo is a great option as well. The game scales the monster down specifically how they engage and allow you buy Grace which allows you to gain extra self-revives for each day.

The story is excellent if you pay attention to the character quests, which reward you with skins, gems, and journal where the lore is told. There are dialogues and scenes to help you understand the world setting, Niightfarers, other elements that go beyond just rushing bosses.

The soundtrack cannot be ignored. It is beautifully designed and fits the game’s theme in every aspect. For instance, the hype goes sky-high during the flights.

System requirement aren’t very high. My five-year-old budget laptop still runs it fine, except for the “Baron” boss which directly attacks the CPU. 

The DLC is also worth it. It meets all my points above and offers more challenges. Even though it isn’t free like the Everdark bosses, the DLC is worth the price for the additional experience in the new underground Limvied and old Limvied.

Overall, ELDEN RING NIGHTREIGN executes marvelously in all aspects and is worth your money and time.

This game has a weird enjoyment curve. First it's fun as you learn routes and bosses and optimize your runs. You get to see a lot of older fromsoft bosses and it can feel like a nostalgia victory lap. You get all the bosses down, all of them being some degree of fun. Then you start realizing how awful the relic drop system is. This is managed to a degree by boss relics which tend to be pretty decent, but to get the better ones you need to defeat everdark bosses, and these are a very mixed bag, with some of them being just straight up awful bosses (ED Libra, ED Augur). Not to mention the 45 minute run back to those bosses. 

You somehow put up with this and see all the content the game has to offer before venturing into the depths. The depths are the worst way of making content harder because it's purely a % adjustment. Enemies just hit harder and have more HP. No different movesets, and the reward pool has even more RNG built into it. It makes the feast or famine aspect way more proeminent, except the fact that when you lose, you lose the equivalent points of 2-3 wins, which just feels extremely punishing. 

To get the best experience out of this game, play it with friends, beat the normal bosses and some everdark ones, and then stop playing. Even at $40, the game feels a bit overpriced for that amount of content. Also, in typical fromsoft fashion, the game has more than a few bugs and clunkiness, which can end up costing you the run.
